dossier.topic: Pine cone scales bend with humidity through discrete fiber bundles in a porous brown-tissue matrix, not a simple bilayer strip
dossier.summary: Pine cone scales open when dry and close when damp, with no living muscle: the cells in a mature cone are dead, so the movement is passive. The textbook picture is a bilayer strip with swelling cells on one face and stiff fibers on the other. A 2025 study finds real scales are multilayered: a sclereid skin, discrete fiber bundles and a porous brown-tissue matrix. Its simulations show a simple bilayer underestimates the bending. Bending concentrates at the scale base, and the drying and wetting paths differ in moisture content.

facts.claim: Dawson, Vincent and Rocca (Nature, 1997) report that pine cone scales gape open when dry and close up when damp, and that the cells in a mature cone are dead, so the mechanism is passive.
Non-serotinous pine cones open when dry and close when wet, and a single cone goes through many opening and closing cycles over its life.
The 2025 study names three tissues in the scale: a sclereid cell layer with the abaxial epidermis, brown tissue, and sclerenchyma fibers.
facts.source_title: Beyond the bilayer: multilayered hygroscopic actuation in pine cone scales

facts.claim: Microfibril angle is highest in sclereid cells, so their longitudinal expansion is higher and radial expansion lower; sclerenchyma fibers have a lower microfibril angle.
facts.source_title: Beyond the bilayer: multilayered hygroscopic actuation in pine cone scales

facts.claim: Simulations in the 2025 study found that discrete fibers embedded in a brown-tissue matrix reproduced the observed bending angles more accurately than a simple bilayer.
facts.source_title: Beyond the bilayer: multilayered hygroscopic actuation in pine cone scales

facts.claim: In the same study's simulations, the maximum displacement was 2.90 mm for a bilayer geometry and 5.57 mm for a scale-like geometry.
facts.source_title: Beyond the bilayer: multilayered hygroscopic actuation in pine cone scales

facts.claim: The study reports desorption-absorption moisture hysteresis at 60% RH of about 2.4 to 2.5 percentage points for each tissue, so drying and wetting follow different paths.
facts.source_title: Beyond the bilayer: multilayered hygroscopic actuation in pine cone scales

facts.claim: A 2025 Frontiers review of cone scale movement reports that in pine the actuator is abaxial sclereids forming a skin, with adaxial fibers clustered in compact vascular bundles, and that during wet-to-dry transition the scale bends mainly in its basal region.
facts.source_title: Hygroscopic movements of cone scale of white fir Abies concolor are tuned by quantitative variation of the scale Bauplan

visualisable_mechanisms.name: sclereid skin over fiber bundles
visualisable_mechanisms.description: The abaxial sclereid skin has a high microfibril angle, so it swells mainly along the scale length when moisture rises. The adaxial fiber bundles have a lower microfibril angle and resist that stretch. The mismatch between the two faces bends the scale.
visualisable_mechanisms.render_or_sonify_hint: A tapered strip: a thin soft band on one face and three to five dark vertical bundles of fine lines on the other. As humidity changes, the strip curls and straightens.

visualisable_mechanisms.name: porous brown-tissue stitch
visualisable_mechanisms.description: Brown tissue sits between the fiber bundles, shrinks less than the sclereid layer and is more porous. It links the bundles into one matrix, so bending depends on bundle placement, not on two uniform layers.
visualisable_mechanisms.render_or_sonify_hint: A dimmer mesh of soft cells filling the gaps between the bundles, with cells that brighten and dim as humidity moves, drawn over the strip's structure.

visualisable_mechanisms.name: basal hinge propagation
visualisable_mechanisms.description: During wet-to-dry transition the bending concentrates in the basal region. Motion starts at the base and spreads toward the apex as the scale dries.
visualisable_mechanisms.render_or_sonify_hint: Over a drying ramp, a bend wave starts at the bottom of a strip and travels upward, so the tip lags the base by a visible delay before it moves.

visualisable_mechanisms.name: open-close hysteresis loop
visualisable_mechanisms.description: Drying and wetting follow different moisture paths, about 2.5 percentage points apart at 60% RH. Plotting scale angle against humidity gives a loop rather than one curve, so each cycle leaves a trace.
visualisable_mechanisms.render_or_sonify_hint: A trail of the scale angle against humidity over repeated cycles, opening and closing paths drawn as two lines forming a loop that thickens with each cycle.

open_questions: How are the fiber bundles and brown-tissue matrix arranged in 3D across a whole scale, and does the layout vary between pine species?
Does the simulation include transient multiphase motion, which the authors list as future work?
How fast does moisture travel from base to apex, and does that set the speed of the basal hinge wave?

surprise.justification: A generalist expects a bimetal-style bilayer strip bending uniformly. Real scales are multilayered: a simple bilayer underestimates the bending, and fiber bundles in a porous matrix set the motion.

brief.title: Basal hinge wave across a grid of pine cone scales
brief.concept: A grid of 48 pine cone scales, each a chain of 12 segments, curls from its base upward as humidity falls, so the bend wave crosses the field from the bottom row to the top.

mechanism_embodied.how_visualised: Each of the 48 strips is a chain of 12 segments. The humidity ramp reaches each segment after a delay that grows with its height, so the bottom segment bends first and the tip lags behind. Each strip shows a pale skin on one face and dark fiber lines on the other. The viewer sees the bend wave cross the grid from base to tip.

brief.discarded_obvious_idea: Obvious: a textbook bimetal strip bending uniformly on a gradient. Rejected: the dossier says a simple bilayer underestimates the bending, and a uniform bend hides the base-to-tip delay that is the mechanism.
brief.motion_sound_plan: High tempo: 48 strips with a cut rhythm of 4 beats and a bend wave paced near 120 BPM through keyframe delays. Warm-consonant: cream ground, ochre and rust, mirrored grid symmetry. Assertive: strips fill the frame, push-in to 1.3x at beat 3, pull-back to 0.8x at beat 4. Experimental: nested-transform segment chain. No sound. Constraint css-only: CSS keyframes and DOM divs only, no script and no canvas.

storyboard.description: Cream ground with 48 strips in an 8 by 6 grid, all upright and open, with dark graphite bases. By 2 s the bottom row has begun to bend at its base while the upper rows stay straight, so the bend front is visible.

The drying wave climbs the grid diagonally from the bottom left. Curled strips form a band across the middle, with tips lagging bases. Skin is rust and fiber lines are graphite. At 8 s the wave front sits mid-frame.
Camera pushes in to 1.3x. Every strip curls closed at full wet, rows packed tight, with an ochre brown-tissue haze behind each strip that brightens and dims with the wave. Peak density and contrast.

Camera pulls back to 0.8x, leaving a cream margin. Strips reopen base first in a staggered wave, and the top row is still curled at 20 s. The grid shows a diagonal open-to-closed gradient that differs from the 2 s frame.

brief.memorable_moment: A bend wave climbs the grid from base to tip, with each strip's tip visibly lagging its base.
brief.self_declared_risk: CSS keyframe delays may not read as a propagating wave across 48 strips, and 12 nested segments per strip may blur the bend curve into a single rotation.
brief.liner_note: Dawson, Vincent and Rocca reported in Nature in 1997 that pine cone scales gape open when dry and close when damp. The cells are dead, so the movement is passive. A 2025 study found the scale is multilayered, not a simple bilayer, and its simulations gave maximum displacements of 5.57 mm for a scale-like geometry and 2.90 mm for a bilayer. A 2025 Frontiers review finds drying bends the scale mainly at its base. On screen each strip is a chain of segments, pale skin on one face and dark fiber lines on the other. As humidity falls, bending starts at the base and climbs to the tip.

evidence.mechanism: shot-02s: 48 upright rust-and-graphite strips in an 8x6 grid, only the bottom row tilting; by shot-08s the arcs curl upward with tips visibly trailing bases, and by shot-20s the top rows still curl while the bottom reopens.
evidence.ambition: shot-08s: 48 nested segment chains render as flat DOM divs with two faces, one rendering idea and no shading, lighting or material beyond rust versus graphite; by shot-20s the pull-back to a cream margin is the only added layer.
evidence.craft: shot-08s: clean flat fills and crisp segment seams, but the fiber lines are near-invisible hairlines and the strips are small on a large empty cream field; by shot-20s the diagonal gradient is tidy without texture.
evidence.distinctness: shot-08s: cream ground with a rust and graphite palette and a grid of bent strips; the look sits close to cream-editorial pieces, and each strip bends by one smooth rotation with no distinct layer or composition.
evidence.polish: shot-02s: composed full-frame grid with the bottom row already tilting; by shot-20s the camera has pulled back to a cream margin and the top row is still curled, so the piece resolves into a diagonal gradient that differs from 2s.

verdict.pairwise_justification: No median archive yet; no head-to-head comparison is possible.
